brief.headline: Microsoft is advertising 2,182 open roles across 55 countries. The largest single strategic cluster is Go-to-Market & Revenue (21.3% of postings), and 40.2% of all postings touch the AI / datacenter / silicon build-out.

sections.title: What the company is staffing for
points: The top three strategic clusters are Go-to-Market & Revenue (465), AI Platform & Copilot (394), Datacenter & Capacity Buildout (371).
1,032 roles (47.3%) build the product, 310 roles (14.2%) build physical capacity, 680 roles (31.2%) sell and serve, and 150 roles (6.9%) run the company.
The build-to-sell ratio is 1.52:1 — weighted toward creating new capability rather than monetising existing capability.
Security appears in 8.8% of postings, indicating it is treated as a cross-cutting requirement rather than a single team.

sections.title: Where the momentum is
points: 1,015 postings (46.5% of the open book) were created in the last 30 days.

Comparing the last three months of postings against the three before them, the clusters gaining share are Go-to-Market & Revenue (16.4% → 22.3%), Data & Analytics Platform (5.5% → 8.2%), Datacenter & Capacity Buildout (14.8% → 17%).

Over-represented in recent postings: Corporate & Enabling Functions (index 1.34), Go-to-Market & Revenue (index 1.22). An index above 1.0 means the theme takes a larger share of new postings than of the total.
Under-represented in recent postings: Azure Cloud Platform (index 0.69), Developer Tools & GitHub (index 0.69), Quantum Computing (index 0.74), Security, Identity & Compliance (index 0.78).
Geographies growing faster than their baseline: China (1.68), Ireland (1.43), Canada (1.39), United Kingdom (1.21).

sections.title: Which organisation is doing the hiring
points: Of the 54.4% of adverts that identify their own organisation, the split by division is Engineering & product divisions 25%, Customer & Partner Solutions 23.4%, Microsoft Frontier Company 6%.
The largest named units are Cloud Operations + Innovation (354), Solution Team Unit (134), Customer Success Unit (106), Industry Solutions Delivery (104), Account Team Unit (78).
Cloud Operations + Innovation (CO+I) alone accounts for 16.2% of the whole open book. Builds and runs the datacenter estate that all of Microsoft Cloud sits on.
Where a commercial solution area is named, the ranking is Security (155), Data & AI (139), Business Applications (125), Azure Infrastructure (56).
Growing faster than their own baseline: Account Team Unit (1.3×), Digital Sales & Digital Natives (1.29×), Global Partner Solutions (1.27×).

sections.title: The named bets
points: Agentic AI is referenced in 420 adverts (19.2%) — by a wide margin the most-cited initiative, and a sign that agents are being staffed as a product direction rather than a research topic.

The "Frontier" language splits in two. 33 adverts invoke the Frontier Firm transformation narrative — reorganising a company around AI agents — while 58 concern frontier-scale model training and the supercomputers behind it. The first is a go-to-market story sold to customers; the second is an engineering one.
Sovereign and regulated cloud appears in 50 adverts, indicating continuing demand from government and data-residency-constrained customers.

sections.title: How the organisation is being shaped
points: Leadership-titled postings (Manager through VP) account for 16.9% of the book; deep individual-contributor titles (Lead/Staff, Principal, Partner) account for 21.7%.
By declared role type the split is 90.4% individual contributor to 9.6% people manager — a flat structure, consistent with deepening existing teams rather than adding management layers.
Early-career and university postings are 2.7% of the book — a modest pipeline, with hiring concentrated on experienced staff.

sections.title: Location and working model
points: 52.5% of postings include a United States location. The next largest markets are India (231), Australia (94), Japan (93), United Kingdom (57).
585 postings (26.8%) list more than one location, indicating roles staffed opportunistically across sites.
Of postings that state a work-site policy, 79.7% require three or more days on-site and 13.4% are fully remote.

outlook: With 40.2% of hiring tied to AI, datacenter and silicon, the advertised plan is capital- and capability-led: Microsoft is staffing to expand the supply of AI compute, not just the demand for it.

The single largest named organisation is the datacenter arm (354 roles). When the biggest identifiable hiring block is the group that pours concrete and racks servers, the constraint being solved is physical capacity, not software headcount.

Agents are the through-line: 19.2% of all adverts mention agentic AI, spanning engineering, consulting and sales. That breadth suggests it is being treated as a company-wide operating assumption rather than one product team's bet.
Engineering is being added faster than field capacity, which usually precedes a product-expansion cycle rather than a revenue-harvest cycle.
The clearest forward signal among the strategic clusters is Corporate & Enabling Functions: it takes 1.34× its baseline share of the last 30 days of postings.
Geographic expansion is skewing toward China, Ireland, Canada, suggesting capacity or market development outside the established hubs.
Since tracking began, the open book has moved -51 roles, with 76 postings opened and 146 closed — net contraction.
caveats: Based only on publicly advertised roles on careers.microsoft.com; internal transfers and unadvertised hiring are not visible.
A posting is not a hire — volumes indicate intent and capacity planning, not headcount actually added.

Business units are resolved from the posting’s structured department where that names the team outright, and otherwise from the way the advert describes itself in its Overview — never from the Responsibilities section, which names teams a role merely collaborates with. About two fifths of adverts resolve; the rest are reported as not stated rather than guessed, so unit totals are a floor, not a census.
The momentum index compares each theme’s share of the last 30 days of postings against its share of the whole open book. Roles that close quickly are slightly under-counted.
Cluster tagging is keyword-based over title, profession, discipline and description, after standard legal and benefits boilerplate is removed. Clusters overlap, so their shares do not sum to 100%.

The Frontier deep dive reads only the adverts that resolve to that organisation, which is a small cohort. Every figure there is therefore reported against the rest of the open book as an index rather than as a standalone number, and its recency window is 90 days rather than 30.

Requirements are read from each advert’s Qualifications block only, and the standard "languages including, but not limited to…" clause is counted as one open-list requirement rather than as demand for each language it names. The month-by-month market lines are survivorship-biased at their early end, since a role posted months ago is only visible if it is still unfilled — the demand index against the whole book is the sounder read.

reading: The Frontier organisation resolves on 130 adverts — 6% of the open book — split Industry Solutions Delivery 104, Frontier Company (unspecified unit) 20, Forward Deployed Engineering 6. A posting resolves either because its structured department names the team or because the advert describes itself as part of it, so this is a floor, not a census.
114 delivery-shaped roles in the cohort are matched by no classified selling role. This does not show whether existing staff or other teams generate demand.

The shape of the hire is Consultant (49, 53.86× the rest of the book), Architect (36, 6.44× the rest of the book), Program & project management (11, 1.67× the rest of the book). 14 postings carry a manager, director or VP title, which is management scaffolding rather than billable capacity.
69.2% of the cohort was created in the last 60 days, against 75.9% of the whole open book. Its hiring is no newer than the company’s as a whole.

17.7% of Frontier adverts commit to an industry vertical, against 12% in MCAPS and 2.6% in the engineering divisions. It is still a minority of the cohort, but it is several times the rest of the company, and it is the clearest evidence that this organisation is structured by market rather than by product. Where a vertical is named it is Financial Services (8), Healthcare & Life Sciences (5), Defense & National Security (4).

Direction of travel by vertical: Government & Public Sector takes 1.73× its baseline share of the cohort's last 30 days, while Healthcare & Life Sciences takes 0.46×. On a cohort this size, read that as a lean, not a trend.
By role shape, Leadership is over-represented in the last 30 days at 2.38× baseline — the clearest near-term signal of what the organisation thinks it is short of.

Against the other two divisions, Frontier is 67.7% consulting-shaped — architects, consultants and engagement leads — against MCAPS 14.5% and the engineering divisions 1.3%. It names an industry on 17.7% of adverts (MCAPS 12%, engineering 2.6%), and of the adverts that state a travel requirement, 18.5% ask for 25% or more (MCAPS 34.9%, engineering 5.1%).

The named capability stack is Azure (76), Copilot (41), Dynamics 365 (28), GitHub (27). Agentic AI is cited on 39.2% of Frontier adverts against 7.7% in the engineering divisions — the delivery arm is talking about agents more than the people building them.

Geographically the cohort sits in 14 countries, led by India (43), United States (34), Japan (12), United Kingdom (9). The United States takes 26.2% of this cohort against 54.2% of the rest of the book — a markedly less US-weighted footprint, which is what a delivery organisation following customer demand looks like rather than one following the product groups.

The language that separates these adverts from the rest of the book is "elite engineers", "organization hosting", "delivery specialists", "existing intellectual" — phrasing about engagements and customer outcomes rather than about shipping product.

A further 40 adverts (1.8% of the book) name Frontier, ISD or FDE without claiming membership — roles told to work with the delivery arm rather than inside it. They cluster in Sales (30), Technology Sales (3), Business Operations (2), which is the surface area the organisation is being wired into.

strategy.title: ISD's future inside Frontier
strategy.scope: An evidence-led reading of possible strategic relevance, not a prediction that ISD will survive, shrink or be reorganised.
strategy.summary: The readable ISD adverts contain signals for make ai work in production; sell industry and business outcomes; scale beyond one-off engagements; connect delivery to lasting adoption; own complex, trusted implementation. These suggest possible ways for ISD to remain useful inside Frontier, not an approved survival strategy.
strategy.method: Only roles classified as ISD are evidence for ISD. FDE is a separate comparison, never folded into ISD. A signal requires a topic and an action in the same passage of Overview or Responsibilities; Qualifications are excluded. When only a published overview excerpt is available, coverage is limited. Counts are adverts, not independent decisions; shared wording is deduplicated in the source examples. These are heuristic text matches, not verified commitments.
strategy.frontierReading: The hypothesis to examine is complementary roles: ISD providing repeatable customer delivery and FDE providing forward-deployed engineering. The comparison below tests overlap in advertised work; it cannot establish a reporting line, a formal hand-off, budget allocation or replacement of one unit by the other.

signals.label: Make AI work in production
signals.inference: One possible role for ISD is turning AI ambition into implemented customer systems, rather than remaining a general-purpose consulting supplier.
signals.risk: AI vocabulary alone does not show production ownership, successful delivery or a profitable services model.
signals.watch: Look for explicit production accountability, operating metrics and customer references, not just more AI mentions.

unknowns: Internal leadership intent, budgets, margins, utilisation and the approved organisation roadmap are not observable in job adverts.
Open postings are not headcount, completed hires or evidence of growth. A missing signal is not proof that a capability is absent.
ISD and FDE classification is heuristic. Compare the linked advert before relying on a unit assignment.
Repeated daily observations can track advertised requirements, but revenue, delivery success and organisational viability need independent evidence.

kpis.label: Ask for the AI stack
kpis.sub: of the last 90 days · whole book 17%

openList.label: Accepts any of several backgrounds
openList.note: "…or related roles" — an enumeration of acceptable histories

reading: 99.9% of the open book states its requirements, and those adverts name 3.1 distinct capabilities each. The capability the market is asked for most often is Delivery & programme (41.3% of adverts), ahead of Cloud & platform (33.4%).

By named skill the ranking is Azure (22.4%), Delivery & programme management (22%), Consulting & advisory (21%), Distributed systems (12.9%), Python (10.8%). Two clauses are deliberately kept out of that ranking because they enumerate options rather than state demands: 48.5% of adverts accept any of several backgrounds ("…or related roles") and 21.2% accept any mainstream language ("…languages including, but not limited to…"). Counted as skills they would be the two largest bars on the page while telling you nothing about what the job needs.

The median entry bar is 3 years of experience, and 86.4% of adverts name a degree. Across the bands the bar runs Intern / entry 1yr, Mid / unspecified 2yr, Senior 4yr, Principal + 5yr, Manager + 3yr — the manager band reads low because what it asks for is years of *people management*, a different clock from the technical bands.

The highest demand indices are Quota & pipeline (1.16×), Construction & commissioning (1.13×), Testing & quality (1.11×), SoC / ASIC / FPGA (1.1×) — each takes that multiple of its baseline share in the last 90 days of postings.
The lowest are Azure certification (0.74×), Security clearance (0.74×), PyTorch / TensorFlow (0.79×), Infrastructure as code (0.79×). On a book this size read those as a lean rather than a retreat.

The AI stack — LLMs, agents, retrieval and model operations — is named in 16.2% of the last 90 days of postings against 17% of the whole book, an index of 0.95. It is holding at its existing level rather than accelerating.

The entry bar moved -1 years across the plotted months (4 → 3 median). Earlier months are a survivorship-biased sample — only roles still open are visible — so read the recent end of that line, not its slope from the start.

The requirements that travel together most often are Azure + Consulting & advisory (216), Consulting & advisory + Customer-facing experience (141), Azure + Distributed systems (128) — those pairs are the shape of the job the market is actually describing.
